cards.en: For five minutes, you've been chatting with two people. Both of their replies seem completely normal. Sometimes a bit of small talk, sometimes a joke, sometimes a personal question. But only one of them is human. The other is an AI. Now you have to decide which one is the person.

In one experiment, when GPT-4.5 was told to talk like an ordinary young person, people took it for the human 73 percent of the time. And here's the surprising part. When those special instructions were removed, that rate fell to 36 percent.

In other words, it wasn't just the machine's answers. Its way of talking was shaping our decision too. But there's a difference here that's easy to miss. Taking a machine for a human, and that machine actually thinking, are not the same thing.

So how do we test whether a machine is only imitating well, whether it understands something, or whether anything is really being experienced inside it? Searching for an answer, we'll travel to an old idea, an extraordinary move in the game of Go, and a locked room.

sections.title: First Question: How Do You Test Thinking?

cards.en: In 1950, the mathematician Alan Turing wrote a paper. It begins with a simple question: can machines think? But he quickly realises that first we'd have to agree on what "thinking" even means. And people could argue about that definition for years.

So Turing takes a different route. Imagine a person who talks with two others only through written messages. On the other side are a human and a machine, but he isn't told which is which. After the conversation, he has to guess which one is the human.
Today we call this idea the Turing test. It isn't a test of looking inside the machine. It judges its behaviour from the outside: in a conversation, can we tell it apart from a human?

That had a real advantage. Instead of fighting over a definition of thinking that nobody agrees on, you could ask a question you can actually observe. But that is also exactly where the test's limit begins. Sounding human is not proof of understanding on the inside.

Think back to a viva, the spoken exam. If a student gives the right answer, the teacher may be satisfied. But sometimes the very next question reveals that the answer was memorised, not understood. With machines, this same difference is going to matter.

sections.title: Second Question: Can a Machine Create Something New?

cards.en: The roots of this doubt go back even before Turing. In 1843, Ada Lovelace wrote about Charles Babbage's proposed machine, the Analytical Engine. It was a plan for a kind of computer that was never finished, but its possibilities were astonishing.

Ada added an important word of caution: the machine makes no claim to create anything new on its own. It can only do what we know how to tell it to do. You still hear this objection today, that a computer, in the end, only runs the rules a human gave it.

Turing took this objection seriously. Part of his answer was that we don't need to write out every possible answer for the machine in advance. Why not build a machine that learns like a child, makes mistakes, and changes its behaviour with experience?

Today that idea sounds ordinary, but it changes the whole debate. The question is no longer which answer the programmer wrote. The question becomes what a machine, after learning, can do that even the people who built it didn't expect.

And then, during a game, a moment came that made some of the world's best experts stop and stare. But to understand it, we first need to see the difference between two very different kinds of computer.

sections.title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected

cards.en: In 1997, IBM's computer Deep Blue defeated the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match. It checked possible moves at enormous speed and weighed up what each one would gain or lose. It was a huge achievement in computing.

In 2016, the contest reached a different game: Go. Lee Sedol, one of South Korea's greatest players, sat down across from AlphaGo, a system built by Google DeepMind. On Go's simple-looking board there are so many possibilities that judging every move just by counting them all is practically impossible.

AlphaGo learned from games played by expert humans, and then kept improving by playing huge numbers of games against itself. So it wasn't just reading from a list of moves written in advance. Through experience, it built up a sense of which decision works best in which situation.

In the second game, AlphaGo played its thirty-seventh move. Today it's remembered as "Move 37". The move was so unusual that the commentators couldn't immediately tell whether it was a mistake, or part of some far-sighted plan.

According to DeepMind, judging by the data from human games, the chance of a human playing that move was about one in ten thousand. But as the game went on, the move's importance began to show. In the end, AlphaGo won that game, and took the whole series four games to one.
This moment isn't memorable because a machine beat a human. What matters is that a learning system chose a strategy that was different from both the habits and the expectations of human experts.

So, is Ada Lovelace's objection settled? Not completely. It did show that machines can produce results we never wrote out for them step by step. But playing a new and winning move is not final proof of understanding that move.

In 1980, the philosopher John Searle explained this same objection with a memorable example. Imagine you're locked inside a room. You don't know a single word of Chinese. To you, sentences written in Chinese are just strange marks.
A slip of paper comes in under the door. Something is written on it in Chinese. You have a thick book of instructions: if you see marks like these, write these marks in reply and pass them back.
You follow the book carefully, step by step. Outside, the Chinese speakers get such fitting replies that they believe someone inside the room knows Chinese.

But nothing about you has changed. You don't know what the incoming note means, or what your own reply means. You followed the rules perfectly, but you never understood the language. That was Searle's question: is arranging symbols according to rules the same as understanding?

One famous reply came back. Maybe the person inside the room doesn't understand, but the whole system does: the person, the book, the rules, and all of them working together. Searle disagreed. He said that even if the person memorised every instruction, he still wouldn't know what the Chinese means.

This debate still hasn't fully ended, and neither side can settle it overnight. But Searle's example at least reminds us that there can be a gap between an answer that looks right and understanding on the inside.

But now a new question comes up. Are today's AI systems also just repeating the rules of some enormous book? Or, while they learn, does some other way of organising information take shape inside them?

sections.title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine

cards.en: To test this, researchers turned to a small game. The game is called Othello. Black and white pieces are placed on a board, and with every new move, the pieces keep changing.

The researchers trained a small GPT-like model on sequences of moves from games. It was never shown a picture of the board, and it wasn't taught the rules of the game separately. All it had was the sequence of moves, and its job was to predict the next legal move.

After plenty of practice, the model got very good at its predictions. Now the real question was this: was it just memorising common move sequences, or did it somehow also know where the pieces were on the board at that moment?

The researchers examined its internal activity. They found evidence that something like a map of the current board was forming inside the model. Information about where each piece might be was there, inside its calculations.

Then they ran another test. They artificially changed the model's internal information about the board, as if one square had been flipped. As a result, the model's predictions for the next moves changed too, to match the altered board.

That strengthened the case that the internal map wasn't just some unimportant side effect. The model was using it to make its next decision. In a small, limited world, it had learned to organise information in a way nobody taught it directly from outside.

But caution is needed here. A small Othello board is not the real world. And evidence of an internal map is not proof of full, humanlike understanding. Still, this result does weaken the simple picture of a machine that only repeats ready-made sentences.

sections.title: Sixth Question: When the Answer Comes, but the Connection Doesn't

cards.en: On the other hand, some of the mistakes large language models make are interesting too. In a 2023 study, researchers found that a model could state a relationship correctly in one direction, yet fail to recognise the very same relationship the other way round.

For example, it may know that Tom Cruise's mother is Mary Lee Pfeiffer. But when asked who Mary Lee Pfeiffer's son is, it may not give the right answer. Of course, people forget things too. But a systematic mistake like this makes us ask how the model actually learned the information.

This problem was named the "reversal curse". In related tests, GPT-4 answered questions about celebrities' parents correctly 79 percent of the time in one direction, but in the reverse direction its accuracy fell to 33 percent. This was a specific test of a model checked in 2023. It shouldn't be taken as a permanent limit of every AI.

Now we have both sides of the picture. In some places, the machine seems to build a working map inside itself, and in others, a simple reversed question confuses it. That's why quick verdicts like "it understands" or "it doesn't understand at all" can go further than the evidence does.

sections.title: Seventh Question: What Does 73 Percent Really Tell Us?

cards.en: Now let's go back to the experiment we started with. The research first appeared in 2025, and was published in 2026 in the scientific journal PNAS. In the experiment, the person asking questions held a written conversation with a human and an AI at the same time. Then they had to decide which one was the human.

When GPT-4.5 was asked to take on the style of a somewhat shy young person who knows internet slang, it was chosen as the human 73 percent of the time. Without that special instruction to adopt the style, the rate was 36 percent. That's why this result reflects not only the model's ability, but also the design of the experiment and its instructions.

The researchers also extended the conversations from five minutes to fifteen. In that separate test, with the same kind of persona instructions, GPT-5 was taken for the human about 59 percent of the time. In other words, in some conditions, even more time didn't make it easier for people to tell the difference.

When people made their decisions, they often paid attention to cues like writing style, the flow of the conversation and personality, rather than deep knowledge or difficult reasoning. Sometimes even a small mistake could make a reply seem more human.

So the strong conclusion from this experiment is that some AI systems can imitate a human very convincingly in a short conversation. But on its own, this experiment doesn't tell us how much they understand inside, or whether they feel anything at all.

Having come this far, perhaps the hardest distinction comes into view. Solving a problem is one thing. Using information about the world around you is another. And feeling something from the inside, having a personal experience, is a third. These three questions are connected, but they are not the same.

For example, an AI can write a beautiful poem about rain. It can say true things about the clouds, the smell of wet earth and the cool breeze. But that doesn't automatically prove it has ever felt the rain.

In 2023, nineteen researchers tried to examine the question of consciousness in AI in a more systematic way. They drew a set of indicators from different scientific theories of consciousness, and then looked at where such indicators show up in AI systems.

According to that assessment, there was no convincing evidence that the systems they studied at the time were conscious. But the researchers also said that building systems with such indicators in the future doesn't seem impossible in principle. And even finding the indicators would not automatically prove consciousness.

So the debate is no longer only about how well a computer can hold a conversation. The question is also what a reliable way to recognise consciousness would even be. When we can't directly see the inner experience of another human being, judging a machine becomes even harder.

sections.title: Ending: What Evidence Do We Need?

cards.en: So, can machines think? Today, instead of answering in a single word, we can ask the question more clearly. Can a machine hold a humanlike conversation? In some experiments, yes. Can it learn, and build a useful map of the world inside itself? In limited tasks, there is evidence that it can.

Does all this mean it understands the way we do, or that it feels anything? On that, there is no decisive agreement yet. Perhaps the better way forward is this: we shouldn't play down what machines achieve, but we also shouldn't draw conclusions from it that we have no evidence for.

And now, the last question is for you. Imagine a machine that talks with you exactly like a human, learns new things, and even corrects its own mistakes. To you, what would be the strongest proof that it is really thinking?
